label: Restauration mondiale des écosystèmes naturels : reboisement, tourbières et zones humides

sources: IPCC AR6 SYR Figure 4.4 — Ecosystem restoration, reforestation and afforestation represent ~3–4 GtCO2eq/yr by 2030
UNEP Decade on Ecosystem Restoration 2021–2030 — Restoring 1 billion hectares by 2030 could sequester up to 13 GtCO2/yr and protect biodiversity
Bastin et al. Science 2019 — Earth can support 0.9 billion ha of additional forest canopy without encroaching on existing agricultural or urban land
IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch.7 — Peatlands store twice as much carbon as all forests combined; their protection is a high-priority no-regrets option

planetary_limits.note: Largest co-benefit of any option in the catalogue; habitat restoration for thousands of species
Mangrove and wetland restoration improves coastal water quality and aquifer recharge

societal_indicators.note: Large-scale afforestation could compete with agricultural land if poorly sited
REDD+ payments to forest-guardian communities transform conservation into local development driver

interactions.note: Halting deforestation is a prerequisite to net ecosystem carbon gains from restoration
Agroforestry targets degraded farmland; ecosystem restoration targets degraded natural land — complementary and non-competing
Both require land area; large-scale BECCS plantations must not displace restoration areas

methodological_note: Largest mitigation potential in the terrestrial AFOLU sector per IPCC AR6 SYR Fig 4.4. Median impact of 3.5 GtCO2eq/yr calibrated against 3–4 GtCO2eq/yr range. High uncertainty (score 3) due to: (1) climate feedback loop — warming destroys the ecosystems being restored; (2) permafrost thaw releasing methane faster than restoration can sequester; (3) risk of poorly-designed afforestation (eucalyptus monocultures in dry zones worsening water stress). Forest delta at 2074 shows +9.5 pp over baseline (restoration of ~350 Mha). Projection baseline: SSP2-4.5.
